title: PH784: Final Exam
text:
← Back to Course Home


Introduction
Read the following article from JAMA Pediatrics as if you were a peer-reviewer of this paper. Note that I chose this paper for this assignment not because it is low quality with many weaknesses—in fact, this is a well-written and high-quality study. However, no study is perfect. The gaps you identify can present good opportunities for future research. This is how each individual (imperfect) study contributes to science.

Aris IM, Perng W, Dabelea D, Padula AM, Alshawabkeh A, Vélez-Vega CM, Aschner JL, Camargo CA, Sussman TJ, Dunlop AL, Elliott AJ. Neighborhood opportunity and vulnerability and incident asthma among children. JAMA pediatrics. 2023 Oct 1;177(10):1055-64.

Briefly, this study examined the relationships between two widely used measures of neighborhood socioeconomic environment and asthma incidence among children at three different life stages (birth, infancy, and early childhood). The neighborhood measures included the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and Child Opportunity Index (COI) at the census tract level. Their main findings are shown in Figure 3 (i.e., adjusted incidence rate ratios, IRRs). In this exam, you will focus on results concerning COI.
Based on what you have learned in the course, critically evaluate the article by answering the questions below. Work alone and do not discuss this exam with classmates.






Tip




Avoid providing unrelated responses and focus on answering the questions you are asked
Each question asks you to discuss multiple points, so make sure you address all of them






Q1
Describe how the authors operationalized the outcome (“asthma incidence”) and discuss the validity of what they assessed as a measure of asthma incidence. If there is a validity concern, explain how the lack of validity may influence their main findings—does it underestimate or overestimate the true effect? Justify your response.






Your answer





Q2
Briefly describe how the COI scores were calculated. Then, explain how they defined and operationalized the “neighborhood” environment exposure based on the COI scores. Discuss the pros and cons of their approach and suggest at least one alternative approach to operationalize neighborhood exposure, including its pros and cons.






Your answer





Q3
Provide the causal interpretation of the adjusted association with asthma incidence for the “very high” COI in early childhood (upper right panel of Figure 3): IRR = 0.80 (95% CI: 0.68-0.94).






Your answer





Q4
Describe the specific exchangeability assumption for causal identification required in this study. Use specific constructs rather than providing a generic description of the assumption. Then, discuss whether you think the assumption is reasonable. Do not just say there may be unmeasured confounders due to the observational nature of the study. First, consider what covariates they controlled for and WHEN they were measured, and discuss whether the control was appropriate. Second, list one potential unmeasured confounder and qualitatively discuss the bias the confounder may induce.






Your answer





Q5
Describe the specific consistency assumption for causal identification required in this study. Use specific constructs rather than providing a generic description of the assumption. Then, describe the hypothetical intervention they are conceptualizing and discuss whether you think the consistency assumption is reasonable. Justify your answer.






Your answer





Q6
Suppose the causal identification assumptions are reasonably met. Instead of the causal estimand the authors used in this paper (i.e., your response to Q3), 1) suggest an alternative causal estimand based on a stochastic intervention for the COI and 2) explain the potential advantages of the new estimand.






Your answer





Q7
Although the authors reported they found no multiplicative effect heterogeneity by sex, race and ethnicity, and rurality, they did not provide the numeric results (which they should have). In general, regression analysis with a product term (e.g., \(race \times COI\)) is statistically underpowered. Suppose they repeated the same study with a much larger sample size and found effect heterogeneity by race and ethnicity where COI is associated with even lower rates of asthma incidence among white group compared to non-white groups. Discuss 1) what might explain this observed effect heterogeneity and 2) the policy implications of the finding (i.e., what insights do you gain from such a finding and how would you use them?).






Your answer

title: PH784: Problem Set #5
text:
← Back to Course Home

Read the following article and answer the questions.

Li S, Stampfer MJ, Williams DR, VanderWeele TJ. Association of religious service attendance with mortality among women. JAMA internal medicine. 2016 Jun 1;176(6):777-85.

https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/2521827


Briefly, this study estimated various “effects” of religious service attendance on mortality. They used data from the Nurses’ Health Study, a large prospective cohort study among US women. They examined both all-cause mortality and cause-specific mortality as outcomes, but we will focus on their findings for all-cause mortality.
They estimated the effects of religious service attendance in 1996 (\(A_{1996}\)) and 2000 (\(A_{2000}\)) on all-cause mortality between 2000-2012 (\(Y_{2000-2012}\)). They controlled for various covariates, including sociodemographic characteristics and health conditions in 1992 (\(L_{1992}\)) and 1996 (\(L_{1996}\)), as well as pre-baseline religious service attendance in 1992 (\(A_{1992}\)), using a method called a “marginal structural model.” Suppose their analysis is based on the DAG below.

Table 2 of the paper shows results of this analysis. For example, the estimate for “At least once per week” in 1996 and “More than once a week” in 2000 was HR = 0.50 (95% CI: 0.46-0.54). This corresponds to the following causal estimand.
\(HR=h(t)^{a_{1996}=1,a_{2000}=1} / h(t)^{a_{1996}=0,a_{2000}=0}\)
where \(t\) is time to the onset of \(Y_{2000-2012}\).


Q1. Explain in words what hypothetical interventions this causal estimand is simulating.






Your answer





Q2. Discuss whether any components of \(L_{1996}\) could be affected by \(A_{1996}\). Justify your answer.






Your answer





Q3. Can we fit a conventional outcome regression to estimate this effect? Why or why not?






Your answer




A critique suggested using the conventional Cox regression for the association between the baseline exposure \(A_{1996}\) and time to all-cause mortality through 2012 (\(Y_{1996-2012}\)), adjusting for pre-baseline covariates (\(L_{1992}\) and \(A_{1992}\)). Suppose the DAG above is correctly capturing the underlying causal structure.


Q4. Notice that religious service attendance is a time-varying exposure. Is the recommended baseline exposure analysis valid? Why? Why not?






Your answer





Q5. When do you expect this effect and the result in Table 2 above (i.e., HR = 0.50) to diverge?






Your answer






Q6 (Optional) How did the authors motivate the use of time-varying exposure analysis via a marginal structural model? Do you find it convincing? Why? Why not?






Your answer

title: PH784: Problem Set #1 (due Sept 15, 2025)
text:
Intro
We will analyze the 2009-2012 NHANES data via the R package NHANES. This document provides a comprehensive info about the package. This package provides two datasets: NHANES and NHANESraw. In the documentation, the following is stated:

NHANES and NHANESraw each include 75 variables available for the 2009-2010 and 2011-2012 sample years. NHANESraw has 20,293 observations of these variables plus four additional variables that describe that sample weighting scheme employed. NHANES contains 10,000 rows of data resampled from NHANESraw to undo these oversampling effects. NHANES can be treated, for educational purposes, as if it were a simple random sample from the American population.

We will use the dataset NHANES (n=10,000) and ignore sampling weights.

Outcome

Continuous: BMI, BPSysAve
Binary: Diabetes, SmokeNow

Social group

Race: Race1
Educational attainment: Education
Income: HHIncome

title: Week 4: Measurement
text:
🗣️ Lecture Overview
Strong study design and fancy statistical methods alone do not ensure good causal inference. Good causal inference requires good data. In this session, students will learn about the importance of high-quality measurements for scientific rigor and properties of good measures. We will then discuss more specific measurements commonly used in social epidemiologic studies, including socioeconomic status and neighborhood characteristics. The session also provides an overview of common and emerging data sources in social epidemiologic research, along with their strengths and limitations.
Key topics covered:

Measurement Quality: Importance of high-quality measurements for scientific rigor
Socioeconomic Status: Measurements commonly used in social epidemiologic studies
Neighborhood Characteristics: Measurement approaches and challenges
Data Sources: Common and emerging data sources in social epidemiologic research

title: PH784 Advanced Social Epidemiology: Methods
text:
About the Course
Methodological rigor is essential in social epidemiology to improve our understanding of the social determinants of health and to inform interventions and policies that promote health equity. Advancing methodological rigor in social epidemiologic research requires an understanding of the unique challenges and key research questions in this field.
This course covers the primary considerations needed to critically evaluate evidence from the social epidemiologic literature and to identify gaps for future research. We will focus on causal estimands, interpretation, and underlying assumptions rather than the statistical mechanics of analytic methods. This is not intended as a general epidemiologic methods course; rather, it provides an overview of recent discussions on methodological issues specific to social epidemiology.

Critically yet constructively interpret causal social epidemiology studies that are likely affected by unmeasured confounders and selection bias

text:
Q4. Discuss potential limitations of their approach to measure “food environment”.
To answer this question, you can read the whole manuscript or only the following quote.

We defined a study subject’s neighborhood as a half-mile (805 m) “network buffer” around his or her residential address, comprising locations reachable within a half-mile walk along the street network.


We derived food environment measures from 2001 data purchased from Dun & Bradstreet (D&B; unpublished data). The data include business name, geocoded location, and detailed Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) industry codes (http://www.osha.gov/pls/imis/sic_manual.html) for food establishments. A priori, we grouped food outlets into categories hypothesized to provide BMI-healthy or BMI-unhealthy food, with one intermediate category for food outlets whose classification was uncertain.


The density per square kilometer of establishments falling within each of these three categories was calculated for each subject’s unique network buffer. Subjects were then categorized into increasing quintiles for each of the three food outlet categories.

Briefly, this study estimated the heterogeneous effects of disaster-related traumatic experiences (home loss and loss of loved ones) on cognitive disability among older adult survivors of the 2011 Japanese earthquake and tsunami. The home loss exposure was binary (0 = no loss or partial damage, 1 = complete home loss), and the continuous levels of cognitive disability were assessed in 2013 (2.5 years after the disaster onset) and 2016 (5.5 years after).
